llm_output.markdown_excerpt: **[Save Your Spot for ValkeyConf 2026](https://events.linuxfoundation.org/valkeyconf)** \| October 5, 2026 \| Prague, Czechia [![Icon Close](https://valkey.io/img/icon-outline-close.svg)](https://valkey.io/) # Documentation: Keyspace Valkey keys are binary safe; this means that you can use any binary sequence as a key, from a string like "foo" to the content of a JPEG file. The empty string is also a valid key. A few other rules about keys: - Very long keys are not a good idea. For instance a key of 1024 bytes is a bad idea not only memory-wise, but also because the lookup of the key in the dataset may require several costly key-comparisons. Even when the task at hand is to match the existence of a large value, hashing it (for example with SHA1) is a better idea, especially from the perspective of memory and bandwidth. - Very short keys are often not a good idea. There is little point in writing "u1000flw" as a key if you can instead write "user:1000:followers". The latter is more readable and the added space is minor compared to the space used by the key object itself and the value object.
